name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,729

clue.text: Old soldier and I might treat SEALs

blocks.note: first meaning: short for veteran, someone who served in the forces
second meaning: an animal doctor, who might treat seals the sea mammals

explanation.surface: A former soldier boasts he could take on the elite US Navy commandos.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make SEALs look like the US Navy special forces, which fits the old soldier; read as the animals, they are patients for an animal doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a clipped form of veteran and the everyday name for a doctor who treats animals.

clue.text: Relations stuck in loo, turning key

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
something stuck in a thing sits wedged inside it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: LAV is short for lavatory
IT is a coy word for sexual relations

explanation.surface: Relatives trapped in the toilet while somebody turns the key in the lock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' suggests family, but here it means sex, which crosswords render as IT. 'Key' sits at the end looking like part of the lock picture; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something key is essential or crucially important, the adjectival sense shared by both words.

clue.text: My wife muses this must change

indicators.note: if letters must change, their arrangement has to be altered into something new

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A husband reflects that his wife is musing that something has to change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muses' reads as a verb about the wife's thinking, but it and 'this' are just the nine letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The missus is informal British slang a man uses for his own spouse.

clue.text: Outgoing old writer seen to be half-cut

indicators.note: cutting something in half removes half of it, so only part of the word survives

blocks.note: EX means former
a pen is a writing instrument
the first half of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: A sociable retired author is seen to be rather drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outgoing' looks like an adjective for a sociable person and half-cut is British slang for tipsy; but the definition is the noun, money going out.
explanation.definitionFit: An outgoing, as a noun, is a sum spent, which is exactly what an expense or cost is.

clue.text: Old flame nowt special? Tell me about it!

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
nothing special means ordinary, unadorned

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a former lover as unremarkable, and a friend sighs in weary agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell me about it!' is usually an idiom of rueful agreement; taken literally it is a request for an account. Nowt is northern English for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, asking someone to tell you about a matter is asking them to give an account or clarify it.

clue.text: Nice to have nothing to do with large yokel

indicators.text: to have nothing to do with
indicators.note: having nothing to do with something means shunning it, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: nice and pleasant are synonyms
L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A snob in Nice wants nothing to do with a big country bumpkin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' at the start of the sentence could be the French city, but it is just the adjective meaning agreeable.
explanation.definitionFit: A yokel is an unsophisticated country person, the disparaging sense of a rural labourer or rustic.

clue.text: Geeks right to punch Celtic hooligans

indicators.note: a punch drives into something, so one piece is driven inside another

blocks.note: ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan, hence Celtic
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Bookish types are entitled to hit Glasgow Celtic football thugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Celtic suggests the Glasgow football club; here it just tells you the hooligans are Scottish, and a ned is a Scottish young tearaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Geeks and nerds are both informal terms for socially awkward, obsessively studious enthusiasts.

clue.text: Tea a medic drugged to get wasted?

indicators.note: something drugged is in an altered state, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor spiked someone's tea so that they would end up intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' looks like slang for drunk or stoned, fitting the drugging, but it means thin from illness or hunger.
explanation.definitionFit: Wasted describes a body shrunk and thinned by disease or starvation, the same sense as abnormally thin.

clue.text: A nincompoop necking nip of nice port

indicators.note: a nip is a tiny amount, so only a single starting letter is taken
necking means swallowing, so one piece is gulped down inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a twerp is a silly person
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fool knocks back a small drink of decent port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' at the end looks like the fortified wine being necked; it is the definition, a harbour city. 'Necking' is slang for drinking quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp in Belgium is one of Europe's largest seaports, so it is an example of a port city.

clue.text: With child, having to inhale oxygen etc.

indicators.note: to inhale is to take something in, so one piece is drawn inside another

blocks.note: with and and both mean together with
a son is a child
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A pregnant woman needs oxygen and similar medical support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With child' reads as one phrase meaning pregnant; split it into 'With' and 'child' to get the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation etc. stands for et cetera, Latin for and the rest, which the English phrase translates.

clue.text: High dudgeon?

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom for great indignation or resentment
setter's reading: anger that happens high up, aboard an aircraft in flight

explanation.walkthrough: 'In high dudgeon' is a stock phrase for being offended; the question mark invites you to take 'high' literally as altitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon is anger, and the term names violent fury by a passenger on a plane, so literally fury at height.

clue.text: I'm told the solver is a beast!

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: the setter addresses the solver as you

explanation.surface: The setter cheekily reports a rumour that the solver is a brute.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often use 'the solver' for YOU, the person the setter is talking to; the female sheep is pronounced the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewe is a female sheep, and beast is a general word for any animal, so it is an example.

clue.text: Capital husband invested in food store

indicators.note: money invested in a business is put inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a deli is a delicatessen
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband has put some capital into a grocery business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money being invested; it is the definition, a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Delhi, containing New Delhi, is the seat of India's national government, so it is an example of a capital city.

clue.text: A pig that mother will feed water

indicators.note: feeding puts food into something, so one piece is put inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
swine is another word for pig
a dam is an animal's mother

explanation.surface: A piglet whose mother will give it a drink of water.
explanation.walkthrough: Dam is the word for the mother of a farm animal, which suits the pig. The definition is a jocular old name for plain water.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a humorous old expression for water, supposedly the only drink the first man in Eden had.

clue.text: Jarring Boris? No flipping singer!

indicators.note: a jarring blow shakes things up, so the letters get jolted into a new order
flipping something turns it over, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's grating voice prompts an exasperated cry that he is no singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' poses as a mild British expletive, as in 'no flipping way'; it is the turnaround signal for the short word.
explanation.definitionFit: Roy Orbison was an American rock and roll vocalist famed for Pretty Woman, so he is an example of a singer.

clue.text: Confuse smack with alcohol? Drop of lager injected!

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the first letter is taken
something injected is pushed inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: bam is the sound of a smack
booze is informal for alcohol
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone mixes heroin with drink, and a little lager is shot in too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like slang for heroin, fitting the injecting; here it is a blow, whose sound is BAM.
explanation.definitionFit: To confuse someone is to baffle or mystify them, which is what this informal verb means.

clue.text: Men on stretch of land in vehicle

indicators.note: placed on means put next to and after, so one piece follows another in an across answer

blocks.note: a tract is an area of land
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers as opposed to officers

explanation.surface: Workers out on a field, riding in some sort of farm vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords use 'men' for OR, other ranks, the soldiers who are not officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractor is a powerful motor vehicle used on farms for pulling equipment, so it is an example of a vehicle.

clue.text: Johnny Rotten was one in charts with a hit

definitions.note: a sentence describing the answer rather than a synonym

indicators.note: something hit is knocked about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Sex Pistols singer once had a chart hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in charts with a hit' reads as a successful pop star; but 'in charts a' are the letters and 'hit' shuffles them. Johnny Rotten fronted the Sex Pistols, whose single was Anarchy in the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: In that song Rotten famously declares himself one who rejects all government and authority.

clue.text: Go wild with game knight having great laugh

blocks.note: RU is rugby union
N is the chess notation for knight
a riot is something hilarious, a great laugh

explanation.surface: A knight goes crazy in a game and has a terrific time of it.
explanation.walkthrough: RU (rugby union) is the usual crossword game; a knight in chess is N because K is taken by the king.
explanation.definitionFit: To go wild is to behave in an unrestrained, uncontrolled way, which is what this idiom means.

clue.text: Indian greeting a Pole in Tyneside

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: Tyneside is in the North East of England, NE
taken as written
a mast is a tall pole

explanation.surface: An Indian person greets a Polish man in Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Pole' look like a Polish person; it is a tall post. Tyneside is the area around Newcastle in North East England.
explanation.definitionFit: Namaste is the Hindi salutation spoken with palms pressed together, a customary welcome across India.

clue.text: Hoskins had to enter contest? That's clear!

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: an event is a competition
Hoskins is the setter, so in his voice this is I had, shortened

explanation.surface: The setter had to take part in a competition, and that is plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name; Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, so 'Hoskins had' becomes I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Something clear in this sense is obvious or plain to see, the same meaning as apparent.

clue.text: A musical combo performing in desert

blocks.note: taken as written
a band is a group of musicians
a performer is on stage

explanation.surface: A group of musicians plays a gig out in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like a noun, the sandy place where the band plays; it is the verb meaning to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert someone is to leave them behind for good, a synonym of the verb meaning forsake.

clue.text: Star workers 'accommodating' American soldiers

indicators.note: accommodating means giving room to, so one piece houses another

blocks.note: worker ants are the classic crossword workers
A is the abbreviation for American
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Top-performing employees put up some US troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star workers' reads as best employees, but 'Star' alone is the definition. Royal Engineers, RE, are the usual crossword soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Antares is the bright red supergiant at the heart of the constellation Scorpius, an example of a star.

clue.text: Ensemble singer arranging Coral hits

indicators.note: arranging puts things into a new order, as with musical arrangements

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A group vocalist arranges the hit songs of someone called Coral.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface makes 'arranging' look like orchestration; it is the cue to shuffle the letters of the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A choralist is a member of a choir, a group of voices performing together.

clue.text: Bishop sat on by copper? Little beast!

indicators.note: in a down answer, one thing sat on by another has it placed above, so the order is fixed

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A clergyman squashed beneath a policeman, who calls him a horrid little brute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a police officer; it is the metal, whose symbol is Cu. In a down answer the sitter goes on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A cub is the young of a bear, lion or fox, so it is a small, immature animal.

clue.text: Some from bar returning judgement in Paris

indicators.note: some from a text is just a portion of it, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run straight through the two words, across the gap

explanation.surface: Barristers come back from the bar with a ruling in a French court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' looks like a reversal signal, tempting you to read letters backwards; it is only part of the host text, and the word reads forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In French law an arrêt is a decision or ruling handed down by a superior court, the equivalent of a judgement.

clue.text: My God, it's tops to be a dog!

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letters are taken

blocks.note: Cor! and My! are both exclamations of surprise
the opening letter of the word
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a dog's life would be the best thing ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My God' reads as one oath, but split it: 'My' alone is the exclamation COR, a British cry of surprise, and 'tops' takes the heads of the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The corgi is a short-legged Welsh herding breed, famously kept by the late Queen, so it is an example of a dog.

clue.text: Like grass? Ruddy yes, European admitted!

indicators.note: someone admitted is let in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: ruddy means reddish
the opening letter of the word
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Asked whether something is like grass, an exasperated speaker says bloody yes, and a European was let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' looks like the mild British swearword meaning bloody; here it means red-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeds are tall grass-like plants, so something resembling them is slender and grassy in appearance.

clue.text: Odd business with a bishop and earl

blocks.note: biz is informal for business, as in showbiz
taken as written
RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's title
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: A strange affair involving a clergyman and an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop in crosswords is often B, but here it is RR, from the title Right Reverend.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd and the answer both describe something strange, weird or very unusual.

clue.text: Old gear shot in arm with ecstasy by tenor

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or broken up, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: An ageing singer injects drugs into his arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot in arm' looks like an injection, matching the ecstasy, but 'shot' rearranges 'in arm' plus E. 'Old gear' is the definition, not the needle.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear is informal for clothing, and this archaic, literary word for clothing is what makes it old.

clue.text: European country finally bans cars

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is taken

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a state is a nation
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A European nation at last outlaws motor vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an estate is what Americans call a station wagon, a car with a long rear load area.
explanation.definitionFit: Estate cars are saloons with extended rear luggage space, so they are a kind of motor car.

clue.text: Have a go at judge?

blocks.note: first meaning: make an attempt
second meaning: hear a case in court and decide it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a go at' sounds like attacking or criticising a judge, but 'at' is just a link between two meanings of one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to attempt something and to examine an accused person in a court of law.
